atoms.text: Many of us see crows nearly every day and most probably don’t notice them. It is most likely that if you live in an area with crows, the crows you see in the neighbourhood are the same crows from one day to the next, and from year to year. But did you know that crows can recognise faces and know who you are?

According to studies, crows recognise faces, categorise them as “friendly” and “evil” and can hold grudges for a long time. In one study at the University of Washington, multiple scientists wore rubber masks, and one netted and captured crows on the university campus. In the following weeks, different scientists would wear the different rubber masks, and the person wearing the rubber mask that captured the crows would get attacked by groups of crows. Even if the person wearing the “evil” rubber mask wore a hat or wore the rubber mask upside down, the crows would recognise the mask and attack the person.

Even over 7 years after the experiment, if someone wore the “evil” rubber mask they would get attacked, and the number of crows attacking increased. Meaning, that even young crows, who weren’t alive during the original experiment, knew about the mask and that it was “evil”.

Crows can also build positive relationships with humans. There have been cases where scientists who regularly left peanuts for crows would be followed. Some even developed friendships with crows, where the crows would bring them small gifts such as stones and coins.
